name: The keyboard map
explanation: The keyboard repeats the same seven white-key names, C through B. The black keys come in groups of two and three — C always sits just left of a group of two.
examples: C is left of the two black keys
F is left of the three black keys

questions.promptText: Which key sits just LEFT of every group of TWO black keys?
questions.explanation: C always sits just left of the two black keys — that's the fastest way to find it anywhere.

questions.promptText: Which key sits just LEFT of every group of THREE black keys?
questions.explanation: F sits just left of the three black keys.

questions.promptText: How many different white-key NAMES are there before the pattern repeats?
questions.explanation: Seven names — C D E F G A B — then the pattern starts over an octave higher.

questions.promptText: You're on C and step UP one white key. Where are you?
questions.explanation: Stepping up from C lands on D — names go up the alphabet as you go right.

questions.promptText: Two keys with the same name, eight steps apart, are called…
questions.explanation: Same name, higher or lower — that distance is an octave.

questions.promptText: Higher-sounding notes live in which direction on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: Right = higher, left = lower. Your ear and the map agree.

name: Beat, bar, and downbeat
explanation: The beat is the steady pulse you'd tap your foot to. Beats group into bars, and the first beat of each bar — the downbeat — carries a little extra weight.

questions.promptText: The steady pulse you tap your foot to is called the…
questions.explanation: That's the beat — everything else in the music lines up against it.

questions.promptText: The FIRST beat of every bar is called the…
questions.explanation: Beat 1 is the downbeat — it's where the bar 'lands'.

questions.promptText: You count '1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4…'. What happens at every '1'?
questions.explanation: Each count of 1 is the start of a new bar — the downbeat.

questions.promptText: If you play a wrong note, the best move for the groove is to…
choices: Keep going and land the next beat
questions.explanation: Musicians keep the pulse. Recover on the next beat — nobody hears the note you didn't replay.

questions.promptText: A metronome is for practicing your…
questions.explanation: The click is an honest timing mirror — that's why the app scores timing, not just notes.

name: Common time — 4/4
explanation: A time signature describes the bar: the TOP number says how many beats each bar has; the BOTTOM number says which note value counts as one beat. 4/4 — 'common time' — means four quarter-note beats per bar.

questions.promptText: In a time signature, the TOP number tells you…
questions.explanation: Top number = beats per bar. In 4/4 you count to four, then a new bar starts.

questions.promptText: In 4/4, the BOTTOM 4 means one beat lasts a…
questions.explanation: The bottom number names the note value of the beat — 4 means quarter note.

questions.promptText: A 4/4 bar so far holds three quarter notes. What single note completes it?
questions.explanation: Three beats are used, one is left — one more quarter note fills the bar.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two-three-four, ONE-two-three-four. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every four beats is the sound of 4/4 — common time.

questions.promptText: How many quarter notes fit in TWO bars of 4/4?
questions.explanation: Four per bar × two bars = eight.

name: Tier 1 check: keys, beats, and bars
explanation: Everything Tier 1 taught, in one short check: the keyboard map, the beat, and 4/4 time.

questions.promptText: Which key sits just left of the two black keys?
questions.explanation: C — left of every pair of black keys.

questions.promptText: In 4/4 time, how many beats are in each bar?
questions.explanation: Four quarter-note beats per bar.

questions.promptText: The first beat of a bar is the…
questions.explanation: The downbeat — count '1'.

questions.promptText: Notes get HIGHER as you move which way?
questions.explanation: Rightward = higher pitch, always.

questions.promptText: Stepping up one white key from E lands on…
questions.explanation: E steps up to F — they're direct neighbors with no black key between.

questions.promptText: A 4/4 bar already has two quarter notes and one half note. It is…
questions.explanation: 2 + 2 = 4 beats — the bar is complete.

questions.promptText: If you miss a note mid-song, you should…
choices: Keep the pulse and catch the next beat
Play it twice to make up
questions.explanation: Keeping the pulse is the skill. Recovery beats perfection.

questions.promptText: Two notes sound in a row and the second is lower. It moved…
questions.explanation: Lower sound = downward movement = leftward on the keys.

name: The staff points the way
explanation: Notes sit on five lines and four spaces. Higher on the staff = higher on the keyboard; bar lines slice the music into bars.

questions.promptText: A melody whose notes climb UP the staff moves which way on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: Up the staff is up in pitch — rightward on the keys.

questions.promptText: The vertical lines drawn through the staff are…
questions.explanation: Bar lines mark where one bar ends and the next begins.

questions.promptText: Two notes on the SAME line or space of the staff are…
questions.explanation: Same position, same pitch — repeated notes sit in one spot.

questions.promptText: From a line to the very next space is a…
questions.explanation: Line to neighboring space = one step (like E to F on the keys).

questions.promptText: A melody that looks like a descending staircase on the staff will SOUND…
questions.explanation: The staff is a picture of pitch: falling shapes fall in sound.

name: March time — 2/4
explanation: 2/4 has two quarter-note beats per bar: ONE-two, ONE-two. Same beat as 4/4, half the bar.

questions.promptText: How many beats fit in one bar of 2/4?
questions.explanation: The top number says two beats per bar.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two, ONE-two, ONE-two. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every two beats is the sound of 2/4 — a march.

questions.promptText: A 2/4 bar already holds one quarter note. What completes it?
questions.explanation: One beat used, one left — a single quarter note fills it.

questions.promptText: Compared with 4/4, a bar of 2/4 is…
questions.explanation: Half the beats per bar — the downbeat comes around twice as often.

questions.promptText: In 2/4, the downbeat arrives every…
choices: Bar line is not a downbeat
questions.explanation: Count 1-2, 1-2 — every second beat starts a new bar.

name: Tier 2 check: reading and meter
explanation: The staff map, bar lines, and telling 2/4 from 4/4.

questions.promptText: Up the staff means which way on the keyboard?
questions.explanation: The staff is a pitch map: up is up.

questions.promptText: ONE-two, ONE-two is the feel of…
questions.explanation: Accents every two beats — march time.

questions.promptText: ONE-two-three-four, ONE-two-three-four is the feel of…
questions.explanation: Accents every four beats — common time.

questions.promptText: Bar lines divide music into…
questions.explanation: Each bar holds the number of beats the top number promises.

questions.promptText: A song starts on beat 2 with the first bar incomplete. That opening is a…
questions.explanation: A pickup (anacrusis) — the Saints starts exactly this way.

questions.promptText: Notes stepping line-space-line-space on the staff are moving by…
questions.explanation: Adjacent staff positions are neighboring keys — steps.

name: Steps and skips
explanation: A step moves to the very next note name (C→D). A skip jumps over one (C→E). Melodies mostly step; chords are built from skips.

questions.promptText: C up to D is a…
questions.explanation: Next-door note names are steps.

questions.promptText: C up to E (jumping over D) is a…
questions.explanation: Skipping one letter name = a skip.

questions.promptText: Chords like C-E-G are stacks of…
questions.explanation: Triads skip every other note — that is why they look like snowmen on the staff.

questions.promptText: E down to D is a…
questions.explanation: One letter down, next-door key — a downward step.

questions.promptText: Most of the Ode to Joy melody moves by…
questions.explanation: It walks to its neighbors — that is what made it your perfect first song.

name: Tier 3 check: moves, positions, subdivisions
explanation: Steps vs skips, the three home positions, and splitting the beat.

questions.promptText: F up to A (jumping G) is a…
questions.explanation: One letter skipped = a skip.

questions.promptText: Two even notes per beat are called…
questions.explanation: Eighths split the beat: count "1-and".

questions.promptText: How do you count four beats filled with eighth notes?
questions.explanation: Each beat gets an "and" for its second half.

questions.promptText: The five-finger position starting on F uses which black key?
questions.explanation: F-G-A-B♭-C — finger 4 rides the black key.

questions.promptText: Moving the same five-finger shape from C to G is called a…
questions.explanation: Same shape, new home — that is the pentascale shift.

questions.promptText: A quick two-note lead-in before a downbeat (like Susanna) is a…
questions.explanation: Pickup notes launch the phrase into beat one.

name: The 1-3-5 recipe
explanation: A major triad stacks the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of its scale: C-E-G, F-A-C, G-B-D. Same recipe, any root.

questions.promptText: A major triad is built from scale degrees…
questions.explanation: Root, third, fifth — the triad recipe.

questions.promptText: The notes of C major are…
The notes of G major are…
The notes of F major are…
Playing E-G-C (the same three notes, re-ordered) gives you…
questions.explanation: Same pitch family = same chord, just re-stacked — an inversion.

name: I, IV, and V — the primary chords
explanation: In any key, the chords built on degrees 1, 4, and 5 are the primary chords. In C: C (I), F (IV), G or G7 (V). V7 pulls home to I.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord I is…
questions.explanation: The chord built on the key note is I — home.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord IV is…
questions.explanation: Count up four: C-D-E-F. IV is F.

questions.promptText: In the key of C, chord V is…
questions.explanation: Count up five: C-D-E-F-G. V is G.

questions.promptText: Which chord most strongly pulls BACK to home?
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh leans hard toward I — that pull ends most phrases.

questions.promptText: Why do musicians name chords by NUMBER instead of letter?
questions.explanation: I-IV-V describes the same relationships in any key — the Nashville idea you'll meet later.

name: Waltz time — 3/4
explanation: 3/4 has three quarter-note beats per bar: ONE-two-three. Amazing Grace, Home on the Range, and every waltz live here.

questions.promptText: How many beats fit in one bar of 3/4?
questions.explanation: Three quarter-note beats per bar.

questions.promptText: You hear: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three. The meter is…
questions.explanation: An accent every three beats — the waltz.

questions.promptText: Which note value fills an ENTIRE bar of 3/4?
questions.explanation: A dotted half lasts three beats — one full waltz bar.

questions.promptText: A 3/4 bar holds a half note so far. What completes it?
questions.explanation: Two beats used, one left.

questions.promptText: The strongest beat in a 3/4 bar is…
questions.explanation: ONE-two-three: the downbeat carries the sway.

name: Tier 4 check: chords and meters
explanation: Triad recipes, the primary-chord family, hearing the dominant lean, and 3/4 vs 4/4.

questions.promptText: The 1-3-5 of F major is…
questions.explanation: F, A, C.

questions.promptText: In C, the three primary chords are…
questions.explanation: I, IV, V = C, F, G.

questions.promptText: The chord that sounds like it is LEANING toward home is…
questions.explanation: The dominant seventh asks; I answers.

questions.promptText: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three is…
questions.explanation: Waltz time.

questions.promptText: G7 adds which note to the G triad?
questions.explanation: G-B-D plus F — the seventh gives it the pull.

questions.promptText: Changing chords WITHOUT breaking the pulse matters because…
questions.explanation: Listeners forgive a wrong note; they feel a broken pulse.

name: Scale degrees: the number map
explanation: The C major scale is C-D-E-F-G-A-B, numbered 1-7. Degrees, not letters, are how musicians think — numbers transpose.

questions.promptText: In C major, degree 5 is…
In C major, degree 3 is…
questions.explanation: C-D-E: E is 3.

questions.promptText: The C major scale uses…
questions.explanation: C major is the all-white-key scale — that is why we start here.

questions.promptText: Where does the right-hand thumb tuck happen in a one-octave C scale?
questions.explanation: Fingers 1-2-3, thumb slips under, then 1-2-3-4-5 to the top.

questions.promptText: The major triad on C uses degrees…
questions.explanation: Chords and scales are the same map — the triad picks 1, 3, and 5.

name: Reading chord symbols
explanation: A letter above the music names a major chord: C means C-E-G. A "7" adds the seventh (G7), "m" makes it minor.

questions.promptText: The symbol "C" above the staff means play…
questions.explanation: A bare letter = that major triad.

questions.promptText: The symbol "G7" means…
questions.explanation: The 7 adds F on top of G-B-D — the leaning chord.

questions.promptText: The symbol "Dm" means…
questions.explanation: A small m = minor.

questions.promptText: Chord symbols mainly help you…
choices: Grasp the harmony at a glance
questions.explanation: Symbols are the fastest map of a song — the notation these genres run on.

questions.promptText: A bar shows the symbol F. Your left hand's most useful single note is…
questions.explanation: The root anchors the chord — bass players live on roots.

name: Finished or asking?
explanation: Phrases end with punctuation: landing on I sounds finished (a period); pausing on V sounds like a question waiting for an answer.

questions.promptText: A phrase that ends on chord I sounds…
questions.explanation: Home is where phrases rest — a full stop.

questions.promptText: A phrase that pauses on V or V7 sounds…
questions.explanation: The dominant leaves the sentence hanging — the next phrase answers.

questions.promptText: Amazing Grace's halfway point parks on G7. That phrase is…
questions.explanation: The hymn breathes at the dominant, then the second half brings it home.

questions.promptText: The very last chord of most songs in C is…
questions.explanation: Endings land at home.

questions.promptText: Hearing where a phrase is heading helps you…
questions.explanation: Phrasing is the difference between typing notes and telling a story.

name: Tier 5 check: degrees, symbols, cadences, waltz
explanation: Everything Arc I taught, meeting in one place.

questions.promptText: In C major, degree 4 is…
questions.explanation: C-D-E-F: F is 4.

questions.promptText: "G7" tells you to play…
questions.explanation: Triad plus the seventh.

questions.promptText: A dotted half note in 3/4 lasts…
questions.explanation: Three beats = one waltz bar.

questions.promptText: A phrase pausing on the dominant sounds…
questions.explanation: V asks; I answers.

questions.promptText: The primary chords of C major are…
questions.explanation: I, IV, and V.

questions.promptText: The C major scale's thumb tuck comes after finger…
Why did every scale lesson end in a riff or fill?
choices: Scales exist to make music, not laps
questions.explanation: A scale is a toolbox, not a lap around the track.

questions.promptText: Melody in the right hand, roots in the left, at tempo, no help — that is the definition of…
questions.explanation: Accurate, in time, unassisted: the standard every tier boss asks for.
